Hi there

I'm struggling with trying to digitise curves on a template? I can successfully create the curves, but adding the curves into the template keeps popping up with an error. How can I successfully add curves into my template, that will be applied to the other specimens? I have tried define.sliders and digit.curves but neither of which I seem to be able to add onto the template.

So far I have this:

locate.lm=choose.dir(caption="template/lm")
locate.sur=choose.dir(caption="template/sur")

file.lm=list.files(locate.lm)
path.lm=paste(locate.lm,file.lm,sep="//")
dat=NULL;aa=NULL;bb=NULL
aa=strsplit(readLines(path.lm)[15:32]," ")
lm.temp=matrix(as.numeric(unlist(aa)),nrow=18,ncol=3,byrow=T)

file.sur=list.files(locate.sur)
path.sur=paste(locate.sur,file.sur,sep="\\")
sur.temp=ply2mesh(path.sur,readnormals=T)
template=buildtemplate(sur.temp,fixed=lm.temp,surface.sliders=Nsl,center=T)

relax_patch=TRUE
{
  folder.lm=choose.dir(caption="Select the folder where the reference landmarks are stored")
  folder.sur=choose.dir(caption="Select the folder where the reference surfaces are stored")
  fil=list.files(folder.lm)
  pat=paste(folder.lm,fil,sep="\\")
  dat=NULL;aa=NULL;bb=NULL

    bb=c(t(matrix(unlist(aa),nrow=Nlm,ncol=3,byrow=T)))

  rownames(dat)=as.factor(gsub("\\.landmarkAscii","",fil))
  array.slide=arrayspecs(dat,Nlm,3)

  atl=createAtlas(sur.temp,template[1:Nlm,],template[(Nlm+1):(Nlm+Nsl),])
  SL=placePatch(atlas=atl,dat.array=array.slide,path=folder.sur,fileext=".ply",relax.patch=relax_patch)

  Y.gpa<-gpagen(SL,PrinAxes=TRUE,ProcD=TRUE,Proj=T,print.progress=T)

Thank you!

messages.body_plain:
Milena,

Neither of these models compares slopes among groups. What you need is a model with individual slopes to a model with a common slope. For ‘size’ and ‘group’ that is:

Y~size*group

Y~size+group

Note that the first model is fully written as: Y~size+group+size:group. The size:group term contains the individual slopes.

For your system it seems you should have:

Shape ~ logcs * Population * Sex

Shape ~ logcs + Population * Sex

Note the ‘*’ and ‘+’ with respect to size and the groups. This determines whether the individual slope terms are present or not.

Dean

I am encountering a couple of errors running the procD.lm and advanced.procD.lm functions, to look at the effect of habitat (flowing/non-flowing - 2 levels), location (river or reservoir where fish are sampled - 11 locations) and sex (3 levels - m, f, immature) on body shape.

y~habitat*sex # no problem here, summary output is given. Same for location*sex.
y~habitat*location*sex # Error in data.frame(df, SS, MS, Rsq = R2, F = Fs) : arguments imply differing number of rows: 9, 7

I'll hazard a guess and say, that the error from the second formula is due to a deg of freedom problem? I'm not sure if that is a problem when using multiple interactions in an ANOVA framework, since there are 3 two-way and 1 three-way interactions for the second formula.
I do have different levels for each factor (i.e. for location, I have 5 reservoirs and 6 rivers; for sex, I have male, female and immature and for some locations, there are only 3-5 males, so that is why I though df or sample size might be a problem).

The other errors occurring using advanced.procD.lm are as follows.

 smelt.shp4<-advanced.procD.lm(smeltshp.gpa$coords~habitat2*sex2, ~habitat2+sex2, groups=habitat2*sex2, iter=99)

I get the following error

 Error in advanced.procD.lm(smeltshp.gpa$coords ~ habitat2 * sex2, ~habitat2 +  :
  Models have same df

So I tried this:
> smelt.shp4<-advanced.procD.lm(smeltshp.gpa$coords~habitat2*sex2, ~habitat2+sex2, iter=99)

But I get the same error:

Error in advanced.procD.lm(smeltshp.gpa$coords ~ habitat2 * sex2, ~habitat2 +  :
  Models have same df

But to no avail:

Error in advanced.procD.lm(smeltshp.gpa$coords ~ habitat2 + location2 +  :
  Models have same df

I have read the R documentation for the function, and tried to follow the model structures in the examples. I also tried including the "groups"  argument, containing the respective interaction of the above models with the same result.

I'm not sure though, if what I'm trying to achieve will work with those structures and the data I have. My variables, in reality, are nested as follows: sex within location, within habitat. Any help is greatly appreciated.

Regards,

Daniel.

messages.body_plain:
Daniel,

You are correct that there is a degree of freedom issue.  How to fix it is not as straightforward as diagnosing the problem.

The error you get from procD.lm is an internal R error caused by trying to assemble an ANOVA table where some values that are expected are missing.  The error you get from advanced.procD.lm is a geomorph error, based on a trap we have set up to prevent pretty much the problem you are introducing.  We find degrees of freedom by calculating the rank of design matrices.  This allows nested designs or incomplete randomized block designs to have appropriate degrees of freedom.  You are using models with interactions, so the functions expect every level of one factor to be found in every level of the other.  This is not correct for nested designs.

You could try something like:

y ~ habitat/sex
y ~ habitat/location + location/sex

to correctly indicate nesting of effects.  I do not wish to suggest that this will solve your problems, but it is a first step.  There could be other issues too, such as your variables being integer or numeric classes, rather than factor classes, misspellings causing extra factor levels (for example, “male” and “Male” are two different levels, where R is concerned), or redundancy between variables (e.g., location offers no additional variation compared to habitat).

The groups argument if for defining which groups to compare in pairwise comparisons and will not help with these issues, which occur “upstream”.  One needs to use advanced.procD.lm for any pairwise comparisons; procD.lm does not perform pairwise tests.

Good luck!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Eudald,

I hope you do not mind but I am sharing my reply to our latest email thread with the geomorph R package list, as the conceptual implications might be of interest to others.

In your integration analyses, you have two approaches: one in which you have two modules and another in which you split one of those modules into two separate modules, thus creating three modules.  To your surprise, but exactly as Dean and I posited below, you had instances where impressive integration with two modules was rendered unimpressive with three (and a few cases where the integration increased when going from 2 to 3 modules).  (For reference, I just compared overall Z scores.)  I’ll try to explain how this happens with one hypothetical example.

If you have two modules and high integration, it does not mean that all Procrustes residuals in one module are correlated with all Procrustes residuals in another module.  It means that at least some are more highly correlated than you would expect by chance with random assortment of landmarks into two modules.  If, by chance or by design, you remove a couple of landmarks from one module and these just happen to be the ones that were highly correlated with some in the other module, now the integration between the first two modules, based on (the Procrustes residuals for) remaining landmarks, is greatly reduced.  It is possible that the third module created is still highly integrated with the second one, but the overall integration is averaged for module comparisons 1-2, 2-3, and 1-3, meaning the overall effect could be greatly reduced.  What one can glean from such an outcome is that the landmarks that were switched from the first module to the third module were probably quite integrated with the second module.

In such instances, it might be wise to do as you proposed: run separate analyses on modules 1-2, 2-3, and 1-3 to ascertain for which groups and in which comparison integration is larger or smaller.  There is nothing wrong with this.  In fact, in my opinion, I would argue that this might make more sense than summarizing integration among all modules as the average of integrations between modules.  (Note, the mean is just one way to summarize this.  One could look at the variance, as well.  Or some other summary measure.  The point is that this is what a single statistic is: a summary.)

Here’s maybe another way to think about this problem.  If one performa a Procrustes ANOVA and determines that there is significant shape variation among groups, is this interesting as a final result?  The answer is probably “No”; rather it is an indication that a test of pairwise means is in order.  What you have discovered in your quest is that it is probably prudent to analyses pairwise modular integrations across pairwise group comparisons.  You can address two questions.  Do I see differences in integration in modular comparisons within groups?  Do I see differences among groups for specific modular comparisons?

Either way, you can use comapre.pls to actually address these questions with hypothesis tests.

Good luck!
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Allometric effect
messages.body_plain:
Marco,

Using the residuals of shape regressed against log size for intergroup comparisons (using ANOVA) or performing ANOVA on shape with log size as a covariate should produce consistent results provided that in the latter, you add the covariate to a model first and use sequential (type 1) sums of squares and cross-products (which geomorph does).

The caveat is important because when using sequential SSCP, the lake effect would be estimated given that the size effect has already been estimated.  Also, keep in mind that the coefficients and SS in an ANOVA table will not be exactly the same with the two approaches, but should be comparable.  The reason for this is with the former approach, one estimates an intercept twice and in the latter, only once.

Finally, if performing the former approach, adding the mean shape to the residuals is a good idea.  This does not change any ANOVA results, but allows one to make TPS deformation grids for e.g., group means, which make sense with respect to the mean shape.

As a personal preference, I prefer using log(size) as a covariate in my analyses and comparing LS means.  I might use the residuals of shape regressed against log size before generating a plot of principal component scores, if visually comparing means is my intention.  (One could also do a between-group PCA.)  But the reason for using it as a covariate is that I can also have a log(size) * group interaction in my model, initially, to ascertain if I should even be comparing means in the first place.  (If significant, then comparing allometric trends is more appropriate.)

Hope this helps!
Mike

Marco,

You did not do analogous approaches in both cases.  In the second case, you compared a model with heterogeneous slopes to one with a homogenous (common) allometric slope, so the pairwise comparisons made little sense (but actually, you were comparing slopes).  Change the second case to

advanced.procD.lm(Shape ~ log(size) + Lake, ~ log(size), groups = ~Lake, slope = NULL, iter=9999)

and you should have analogous results.

NOW HAVING SAID THAT….

I recommend you stick with you second approach because as it demonstrates, you have heterogenous slopes.  There is no way to do an allometric correction, as you did in the first case, because the slopes are different.

You can also use procD.allometry to generate some helpful plots to understand how slopes might be different, but it looks like you have a combination of angular differences in allometric slopes between lakes (organisms change shape as they grow in different ways) and vector length differences (in some lakes, organisms change shape more as they grow).

YOU CANNOT COMPARE MEANS BECAUSE DIFFERENCES IN SHAPE ARE DIFFERENT AT SMALL AND LARGE SIZES.

As you alluded, having only juveniles in some cases means you really have to examine the different allometric patterns rather than try to merely adjust for them.

Good luck!
Mike

Eudald,

I hope you do not mind but I am sharing my reply to our latest email thread with the geomorph R package list, as the conceptual implications might be of interest to others.

In your integration analyses, you have two approaches: one in which you have two modules and another in which you split one of those modules into two separate modules, thus creating three modules.  To your surprise, but exactly as Dean and I posited below, you had instances where impressive integration with two modules was rendered unimpressive with three (and a few cases where the integration increased when going from 2 to 3 modules).  (For reference, I just compared overall Z scores.)  I’ll try to explain how this happens with one hypothetical example.

If you have two modules and high integration, it does not mean that all Procrustes residuals in one module are correlated with all Procrustes residuals in another module.  It means that at least some are more highly correlated than you would expect by chance with random assortment of landmarks into two modules.  If, by chance or by design, you remove a couple of landmarks from one module and these just happen to be the ones that were highly correlated with some in the other module, now the integration between the first two modules, based on (the Procrustes residuals for) remaining landmarks, is greatly reduced.  It is possible that the third module created is still highly integrated with the second one, but the overall integration is averaged for module comparisons 1-2, 2-3, and 1-3, meaning the overall effect could be greatly reduced.  What one can glean from such an outcome is that the landmarks that were switched from the first module to the third module were probably quite integrated with the second module.

In such instances, it might be wise to do as you proposed: run separate analyses on modules 1-2, 2-3, and 1-3 to ascertain for which groups and in which comparison integration is larger or smaller.  There is nothing wrong with this.  In fact, in my opinion, I would argue that this might make more sense than summarizing integration among all modules as the average of integrations between modules.  (Note, the mean is just one way to summarize this.  One could look at the variance, as well.  Or some other summary measure.  The point is that this is what a single statistic is: a summary.)

Here’s maybe another way to think about this problem.  If one performa a Procrustes ANOVA and determines that there is significant shape variation among groups, is this interesting as a final result?  The answer is probably “No”; rather it is an indication that a test of pairwise means is in order.  What you have discovered in your quest is that it is probably prudent to analyses pairwise modular integrations across pairwise group comparisons.  You can address two questions.  Do I see differences in integration in modular comparisons within groups?  Do I see differences among groups for specific modular comparisons?

Either way, you can use comapre.pls to actually address these questions with hypothesis tests.

Good luck!
Mike
